t: Nucleation, and why most crystals never happen
s: Find out how rare a crystal actually is. Clusters flicker into existence and dissolve at random until one happens to cross the critical radius and runs away. Push the supersaturation up and watch the survival rate climb. SENDS the survivor count onward

t: Crystal growth, with a gravity you can turn down
s: Find out why taking gravity away makes a crystal grow slower rather than faster. Four linked views. Turn gravity down and a depleted shell builds up around the crystal until growth is limiting itself. Péclet crosses one on the way and you can find it yourself. TAKES a seed count from nucleation · SENDS a radius and a declared strain proxy onward

t: The phase diagram, as a set of instructions
s: Find out what is actually in the beaker. Drag a point around a binary diagram and read off which phases are present and in what proportion, rather than treating the diagram as a picture.

t: Solidification, and what a phase diagram is for
s: Find out what a composition does to a microstructure. Choose one, press cool, and watch it form beside the diagram: dendrites at one composition, eutectic lamellae at another. Same alloy, same cooling, different material.

t: The stalactite, with and without gravity
s: Find out what she thinks happens and where the evidence stops. Under gravity a drop forms, stretches and falls, and a spike builds downward. Beside it, at almost no gravity, the drop never falls. The prediction is dated and the box next to it is empty because she has not found the paper.

t: Thin film interference, and why a bubble has colours
s: Find out where a colour comes from when there is no pigment. Drag the thickness and watch the reflected colour sweep the spectrum. Put glass behind the film and it becomes an anti reflection coating, and the quarter wave condition is findable by hand.

t: Band gaps, and which light gets through
s: Find out why a material is transparent to some light and not to other light. Drag the wavelength. A photon only lifts an electron across if it carries enough energy, and below that the material simply lets it past.

t: Where the sunlight actually goes
s: Find out how much of the sun a solar cell throws away before anything electrical happens. The real measured spectrum with a band gap cutting it in two: light too weak to be absorbed, and energy dumped as heat the instant it is. SENDS the band gap onward · integrated from the NREL table, not sketched

t: The Shockley-Queisser limit, and a second junction
s: Find out why one solar cell cannot beat about a third, and what a second junction underneath does about it. Detailed balance on that same spectrum, giving 33.7 percent at 1.34 eV, then 45.7 percent for a current matched tandem. TAKES a band gap from the spectrum above it

t: Thermoelectrics, and the argument the field is having
s: Find out why the field is hard. You want electrical conductivity high and thermal conductivity low, and in most materials the same carriers do both, so improving one damages the other. Watch the two figures fight as you dope it.

t: Powder diffraction, and reading a pattern
s: Find out how a structure is actually identified. The full pattern for a chosen lattice, peaks at their correct angles with the responsible planes named, and the systematic absences that do the identifying. Then it turns around and asks you which lattice produced a pattern. TAKES a crystal from the growth simulation · Williamson-Hall separates size from strain

t: Bragg's law, one reflection at a time
s: Find out what a diffraction peak is, before there is a pattern of them. Two X rays off neighbouring planes. Move the angle and the spacing until the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths, which is the moment a detector sees anything at all.

t: Unit cells you can turn over
s: Find out what the packing of a lattice actually means. Turn a cell over and count what is inside it, which is the step everybody skips and then cannot do later.

t: A metal organic framework you can turn over
s: Find out why a wider pore is a worse sieve. Metal nodes, organic linkers and the hole between them, which is the point of the material. Swap in a longer linker and watch the aperture open until everything on the gas list passes, which separates nothing.

t: Titration, drop by drop
s: Find out what picking the wrong indicator costs you. The curve draws itself as the drops fall. Switch to a weak acid and the buffer region appears. Put methyl orange against it and the reading comes out ninety one percent early, and looks perfectly reasonable.

t: Why the pH scale is logarithmic
s: Find out why the scale exists at all. The same number on a linear axis and a log axis, side by side. The linear bar disappears, and that is the whole argument.

t: Arrhenius, plotted twice
s: Find out what linearising a curve buys you. Rate against temperature is a curve you cannot read anything off. The log of it against one over temperature is a straight line whose slope hands you the activation energy. Same data, both ways, at once.
